strengths: Forecasting pretraining loss from partial runs addresses a relevant NLP problem. Modeling losses by token position provides an interpretable empirical perspective on training dynamics.

The experiments cover 468M and 1.2B models trained on 400B tokens, with both Pile and C4 validation data. The reported positionwise fits and forecasting results from 10–40% training prefixes provide promising evidence within these settings.
The data-mixture application improves perplexity in all four reported settings and downstream accuracy in 12 of 14 comparisons. These results provide preliminary evidence of practical usefulness.

The manuscript supplies explicit equations, model configurations, package versions, and additional empirical plots. Appendix B.3 also clarifies that the weighting interventions preserve average loss weight.
weaknesses: The central power-law comparison requires correction or explanation. Table 1 reports strongly negative R² for fits to the complete trajectories, although the stated family L=(p1*x)^p2+p3 includes a constant predictor when p2=0. Under the described unconstrained least-squares objective, the best fit therefore cannot perform worse than predicting the mean. Failed optimization, undisclosed constraints, or a reporting error must be ruled out before these results can establish that power laws fail.

The experiments do not isolate the benefit of token-position decomposition. Once a0 and a1 are frozen, Equations 8–10 reduce the overall loss to a constant plus a cosine. The proposed predictor explicitly incorporates the learning-rate schedule, while its baselines lack this information. A direct aggregate-loss predictor with the same piecewise logarithmic/cosine structure is an essential control for the claimed advantage.

The evidence supports a narrower empirical relationship than the general temporal-law framing suggests. Both model sizes use the same corpus, context length, training horizon, and cosine schedule. OOD validation tests a different text distribution, but not robustness across training regimes. The functional forms are also developed and evaluated on the same small collection of trajectories; independent runs and variation in schedule or horizon would strengthen the forecasting claim.

The hyperparameter-selection evidence is incomplete. Selection uses 10B tokens, only 2.5% of the 400B-token horizon, whereas Figure 3 evaluates forecasting from 10–40%. Predicted and realized losses for all five candidates, ranking accuracy, and errors at the actual selection budget are missing. The modest perplexity gains lack uncertainty estimates; averaging five neighboring checkpoints does not measure variation across independent training runs. Appendix B.2 also uses the reported benchmark suite for candidate selection without describing a separate evaluation split.

Important reproduction details remain unspecified: nonlinear-solver initialization and bounds, the outlier-rejection rule, checkpoint sampling, and the exact candidate mixtures and search budget. No fitting-code or loss-trajectory release is linked. These omissions are particularly consequential given the anomalous baseline fits.

The conclusion that position reweighting is unnecessary exceeds the evidence. Equation 17 follows from manually freezing two fitted parameters; Figure 6 supplies useful descriptive corroboration, but equal loss-decrease rates do not establish that changing training weights cannot help. Testing three fixed suppression strategies supports a limited empirical conclusion, not the broader theoretical justification claimed.
